newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: Lithuanian elections hit by voter apathy.
newsitem.headline: Lithuanian elections hit by voter apathy.

text.p: Lithuania awaited results on Monday from its second parliamentary elections since quitting the former Soviet Union, with voter aparthy overshadowing a comeback bid by independence hero Vytautas Landsbergis.

Opinion polls showed Landsbergis and his Homeland Union had a good chance of winning power from the ex-Communists of the Lithuanian Democratic Labour Party (LDLP), but voters delivered a snub to him and other politicians by turning out in low numbers.
Landsbergis spearheaded the Baltic state's independence drive from Moscow in a struggle that helped bring down the whole Soviet empire.
But a shock reversal at elections in 1992 saw voters dump him as the economy collapsed.
Turnout figures showed Lithuanians had failed to get excited about Sunday's elections. With two hours of voting to go, just over 50 percent of the electorate had turned out.
This was well down on the 70 percent level at the same stage of the 1992 elections.
Total turnout in 1992 was 75 percent but those elections came at a time of economic collapse and political confusion.
Landsbergis was quick to blame the voter apathy on four years of rule by the ex-Communists.
"It indicates disappointment with democratic institutions...It is the bad result of a bad job," he told Lithuanian television.

Sunday's vote was the first round of the elections, with a run-off set for November 10. The first round will decide 70 of the 141 parliamentary seats under a proportional system and the second round the rest under a majority vote.
First results were expected after 2 a.m. on Monday (2300 GMT on Sunday).
Political commentators had predicted Lithuanians might choose to register a protest against established political parties for failing to provide new ideas.

Many people say they have failed to notice big changes in their lives six years after quitting the former Soviet Union. They are also fed up with the seeming lack of choice between the Homeland Union and the LDLP.
Opponents have accused the LDLP of reneging on its promises of easing the pain of economic reforms.
Instead the party followed a path of austerity along International Monetary Fund (IMF) guidelines.
It was badly hurt at the end of last year when a former prime minister withdrew his funds from a bank days before it was shut at the start of a banking crisis.
Foreign Minister Povilas Gylys, a leading LDLP figure, blamed the low turnout on general pessimism.
"Many of our former supporters are disillusioned because they do not see improvements in their social security," he said.
A low turnout was thought to favour the Homeland Union, whose supporters tend to vote early and are more disciplined.
Opinion polls had suggested the Homeland Union would become the largest party in parliament but would not get enough votes to form a government on its own.
The Homeland Union has said it will work with the Christian Democrats, who stress traditional values in this Roman Catholic country.
Cheslovas Jurshenas, LDLP speaker of parliament, said there was a difference between the 1992 and 1996 elections.
"This time all was quiet," he said on television. "This is all about the charm and the lessons of democracy."
